In nineteen nineteen, a wave of molasses hit Boston at thirty five miles an hour.
It was a mild January day in the North End.
Over the street stood a giant tank, fifty feet tall, packed with more than two million gallons of molasses.
The tank had one little problem. It leaked.
So much, that neighbors filled their cups with the sticky drips.
The company's fix? They painted it brown.
Then, right after lunch, the tank groaned. And burst.
A wall of molasses, taller than a house, rolled down the street.
It knocked buildings off their foundations. Twenty one people did not survive.
You see, the tank had been warning everyone for days.
Think of the little yellow light on your car dashboard. The one you cover with tape.
Cars don't write letters. They send lights.
A warning you can paint over is still a warning.
The families sued, and the court called in real experts. After that, new safety rules came for builders and engineers.
People say, slow as molasses. Nobody told the molasses.
